decks.module: Exam parts and who must test
decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: What are the four parts of the Missouri driver examination?
cards.back: The Missouri driver examination has four parts: a written test on traffic laws and safe-driving rules, a vision test, a road sign test and a driving skills test.

cards.front: In which three situations is the Missouri driver examination required?
cards.back: The examination is required for a new Missouri license, for a Missouri license expired more than six months (one hundred eighty-four days), and whenever the Director of Revenue asks, even if your license is current.

cards.front: Which license revocations send a driver back through the examination?
cards.back: A license revoked for too many points or for an Administrative Alcohol action also sends the driver back through the examination.

cards.front: Which out-of-state drivers take only the vision and road sign tests?
cards.back: A driver whose license from another state is valid or expired less than one hundred eighty-four days, applying for the same type of Missouri license, takes only the vision and road sign tests.

cards.front: What two conditions must an out-of-state license meet for the shortened route?
cards.back: An out-of-state license qualifies for the shortened vision and road sign route only if it is for the same type of license and is valid or expired less than one hundred eighty-four days.

cards.front: Who gives the Missouri driver examination, and who can point you to a testing center?
cards.back: The Missouri State Highway Patrol (MSHP) gives the driver examination, and either the MSHP or the Department can point you to the nearest testing center.

cards.front: What must you prove before the exam, and when do you show that identification again?
cards.back: You must prove your legal name and age before the exam, and you show that identification again whenever you apply for a license or permit and each time you take the written or driving test.

cards.front: Where can you find Department and Highway Patrol phone numbers and testing locations?
cards.back: The phone numbers for the Department and the Highway Patrol are printed at the back of the guide, and testing locations are also listed on the Highway Patrol website.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: What format and length does the Class F written test have?
cards.back: The Class F written test has twenty-five multiple-choice questions on the laws and driving methods this guide covers.

cards.front: Is the Class F written test open book, and is the commercial vehicle chapter on it?
cards.back: The written test is not open book, and a Class F applicant is not tested on the commercial vehicle material in Chapter fifteen.

cards.front: How does the written test differ for a Class E for-hire applicant?
cards.back: A Class E for-hire applicant takes a special written test that adds the Chapter fifteen commercial vehicle material, and it is also not open book.

cards.front: How do the Class F and Class E written tests differ, and what do they share?
cards.back: Both the Class F and the Class E written tests are closed book; the difference is that only the Class E test includes the commercial vehicle chapter.

cards.front: What does the road sign test check?
cards.back: The road sign test checks whether you can recognize traffic signs and understand what they mean.

cards.front: What kinds of exam fraud are punished, and how?
cards.back: Fraud in any license, permit or nondriver ID examination, such as false statements, cheating, or using a recording, camera or two-way communication device, is a Class A misdemeanor that can cost your driving privilege for up to one year.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: Which two vision tests does every new or renewal applicant take?
cards.back: Every new or renewal license or permit applicant takes both an acuity test and a peripheral (side) vision test.

cards.front: What is the standard minimum acuity for a Missouri license?
cards.back: The standard minimum acuity is twenty over forty or better using either eye or both eyes.

cards.front: Does passing the acuity screen also cover side vision?
cards.back: The twenty over forty figure is the standard passing acuity, while a separate peripheral test measures side vision, so passing one screen does not cover the other.

cards.front: What is the standard minimum side vision for a Missouri license?
cards.back: The standard minimum side vision is fifty-five degrees or more in each eye, or eighty-five degrees or more in one eye.

cards.front: What are the two passing routes for side vision, and what is the floor below which no license is possible?
cards.back: Side vision has two passing routes, fifty-five degrees in each eye or eighty-five degrees in a single eye, while seventy degrees combined is the floor below which no license is possible.

cards.front: What can happen if you miss the vision standards?
cards.back: Missing the vision standards can lead to a denied license or to restrictions placed on the license.

cards.front: What happens if you fail the standard vision test at the exam?
cards.back: If you fail the standard vision test, the examiner hands you a vision exam form for an eye specialist or physician, and a new prescription may mean waiting for the glasses or contacts before the written or driving test.

cards.front: Below which vision levels can you neither take the driving test nor hold a Missouri license?
cards.back: If both natural and corrected acuity are worse than twenty over one hundred sixty, or combined side vision is worse than seventy degrees, you cannot take the driving test or hold a Missouri license.

cards.front: Is twenty over one hundred sixty the standard passing acuity?
cards.back: The twenty over one hundred sixty acuity cutoff applies only when both natural and corrected vision are worse than it; it is the point at which a license is impossible, not the standard passing level.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: When is the driving test given, and by whom?
cards.back: The driving test comes only after the written, vision and road sign tests are passed, and it is given by an MSHP driver license examiner.

cards.front: What does the examiner check about the test vehicle, and when is the test refused?
cards.back: The examiner inspects the test vehicle for required equipment and safe condition, and the test is refused if the vehicle is not properly equipped or testing seems dangerous.

cards.front: Which plates, sticker, belts, doors and seat does the test vehicle need?
cards.back: The test vehicle needs current plates, a valid inspection sticker, working seat belts, working doors for the driver and the examiner, and a clean, safe passenger seat.

cards.front: Which brakes, warning device and paperwork must the test vehicle also have?
cards.back: The test vehicle also needs a working parking brake and foot brake, a working horn, and proof of financial responsibility.

cards.front: Who rides during the driving test, and how should you behave?
cards.back: Only you and the examiner ride during the test; skip needless conversation, remember the examiner is there to test rather than teach, and obey every Missouri traffic law.

cards.front: After the examiner gives a direction, how much time do you have?
cards.back: After the examiner gives a direction, you are allowed enough time to check traffic and carry it out.

cards.front: When asked to use a control such as the wipers, what are you graded on?
cards.back: When asked to use controls such as the accelerator, brakes, turn signals and wipers, you are graded on finding each one without searching and using it correctly.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: What are you graded on when you pull away from the curb?
cards.back: When you pull away you are graded on starting the car, releasing the parking brake, checking that the way is clear, signaling, and driving smoothly at the right speed.

cards.front: How are starting and stopping graded?
cards.back: Starting and stopping are graded for smoothness and safety, reaction time and control of the car while stopping.

cards.front: How large is the space used for the parallel parking task?
cards.back: The parallel parking task uses a space twenty-five feet long and seven feet wide.

cards.front: What curb distance, position and time limit are scored in parallel parking?
cards.back: Parallel parking is scored on stopping no more than eighteen inches from the curb, near the middle of the space, and finishing within two minutes.

cards.front: Besides distance and time, what else is scored in parallel parking?
cards.back: Parallel parking is also scored on your position before backing, not touching the space markers, turning the wheels the right way, and checking traffic and signaling before pulling out.

cards.front: Which parking task has a time limit and a marked space?
cards.back: Only parallel parking carries a time limit, two minutes, and only it uses a marked space, twenty-five feet long by seven feet wide.

cards.front: How must you look and drive when backing on the test?
cards.back: When backing, you look over your right shoulder through the rear window and must keep a straight line, stay in the proper lane and hold the right speed.

cards.front: How many turns do you make on the test, and what is graded?
cards.back: You make at least two right turns and two left turns, graded on lane choice, timely signals, turning into the proper lane, traffic checks, speed and control.

cards.front: What is the minimum number of each kind of turn on the test?
cards.back: For the turning task you make a minimum of two right and two left turns.

cards.front: What is scored when you park on a hill during the test?
cards.back: Parking on a hill is graded on stopping no more than eighteen inches from the curb, leaving the car in park or the correct gear, turning the front wheels correctly, setting the parking brake, then checking traffic and signaling.

cards.front: What curb-distance limit do parallel parking and hill parking share?
cards.back: Parallel parking and hill parking use the same curb-distance limit of no more than eighteen inches.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: What are you graded on at intersections?
cards.back: At intersections you are graded on obeying signs and lights, approach speed, awareness of traffic, lane position, yielding without blocking traffic, and a full stop at the proper place for stop signs.

cards.front: Which two intersection behaviors are singled out in the intersection task?
cards.back: The intersection task includes making a full stop at the proper place at stop signs and yielding without blocking other traffic.

cards.front: What does the examiner watch throughout the whole test?
cards.back: Throughout the test the examiner also watches your following distance, speed, lane use and lane markings, traffic awareness and yielding.

cards.front: What does the examiner grade about traffic signs and signals throughout the drive?
cards.back: The examiner also grades whether you notice and obey traffic signs and signals throughout the drive.

decks.domain: The Missouri driver examination: written, vision, road sign and driving skills tests

cards.front: How does the point system decide a failed driving test?
cards.back: The examiner deducts points for driving errors, and losing more than thirty points fails the driving test.

cards.front: Which errors fail the driving test at once?
cards.back: You fail at once for an at-fault crash with another vehicle, hitting a pedestrian, driving so dangerously a crash could have resulted, breaking a traffic law, or refusing to drive as directed.

cards.front: Can you fail the driving test without reaching the point limit?
cards.back: A test can be failed outright without reaching the point limit, for example by breaking a traffic law or refusing an instruction.

cards.front: What do you receive for passing, and can you drive on it?
cards.back: Passing earns a test results form, but that form is not valid for driving; you must first apply for and receive a license at a license office.

cards.front: How many driving tests may you take in one day?
cards.back: Only one driving test may be taken per day, and the examiner will suggest practice before a retest.

cards.front: What is required after three failed driving tests?
cards.back: After three failed driving tests, no further test is allowed without written Department authorization, and you must complete extra behind-the-wheel training, send proof, and receive approval to test.

cards.front: How do the point limit and the failure count differ?
cards.back: The point limit and the failure count are different numbers: losing more than thirty points fails a single test, while three failed tests trigger the Department authorization and extra training requirement.

cards.front: Where do failed driving test results go, and what follows?
cards.back: Results of failed driving tests are sent to the Department of Revenue, which then mails a letter requiring additional behind-the-wheel training.

cards.front: Who must give the extra training after three failures, and what is needed before the next attempt?
cards.back: The extra training after three failures must be given by an eligible driver, and you must hold Department approval to test before the next attempt.

recaps.module: Exam parts and who must test

recap_hooks.text: The examination has four parts, and it is required for new licenses, long-expired ones, some revocations, or when the Director asks.
A recent out-of-state license of the same type takes only the vision and road sign tests.
The Highway Patrol gives the examination, and you prove your name and age each time you test.
The Class F written test is twenty-five multiple-choice questions, closed book, without the commercial chapter.
The Class E test is also closed book but adds the commercial chapter, and exam fraud is a Class A misdemeanor.
The road sign test checks that you recognize signs and know what they mean.
Acuity and side vision are separate screens: twenty forty or better, and fifty-five degrees each eye or eighty-five in one.
Below twenty one-sixty acuity or seventy degrees combined side vision, no license is possible.
A failed screen means a form for an eye specialist and possibly a denied or restricted license.
The driving test comes last, in a vehicle the examiner inspects for plates, sticker, belts, doors, brakes, horn and insurance proof.
Only you and the examiner ride, you get time to carry out directions, and controls are graded on finding and using them.
Parallel parking uses a marked space, eighteen inches from the curb, finished within two minutes.
Hill parking shares the eighteen-inch limit, and you make at least two right and two left turns.
Pulling away, starting, stopping and backing are graded on checks, signals, smoothness and control.
At intersections you obey signs and lights, yield without blocking traffic and stop fully at the proper place.
All through the drive the examiner watches spacing, speed, lanes, awareness, yielding and signs.
Losing more than thirty points fails a test, and some errors fail it at once.
Passing earns a results form, not a license, and only one test is allowed per day.
Three failures require extra training from an eligible driver and Department approval to test.
